system.star: Hearth, a K3V orange dwarf (0.75 M☉, 0.22 L☉, 4,650 K)

facts.claim: Hearth is a K3V dwarf of 0.75 solar masses and 0.22 solar luminosities, with a 4,650 K photosphere whose output peaks near 620 nm and is weak in UV-B.
facts.justification: A cool, old, quiet main-sequence star buys tens of billions of years of stable irradiation and a red-shifted spectrum, so evolution can be slow and exposed surfaces need less UV shielding than on Earth; the flare rate is highly speculative without an age and rotation model, since K dwarfs quieten as they spin down.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Photosystems must harvest orange-red light, not blue.
UV-B at the surface is about a third of Earth's, so exposed skin is survivable but not free.
Flare-driven UV spikes, whatever their true frequency, select for DNA repair pathways.

facts.claim: The planet orbits at 0.52 AU with a 158-day year, receiving 0.81 times Earth's insolation.
facts.justification: Flux falls as 1/a², so 0.22 L☉ at 0.52 AU gives 0.81 S and Kepler's third law for 0.75 M☉ fixes the year at 158 days; the 286 K mean is model-dependent, because an albedo of ~0.25 alone yields an equilibrium temperature near 246 K and the rest must come from a CO₂/H₂O greenhouse under 1.5 bar.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Seasons are short: a full wet-dry cycle passes in about five months.
Mean surface temperature sits near 286 K, cool enough to favour large, well-insulated ectotherms.
Mild insolation plus a 1.5-bar atmosphere keeps liquid water stable without a runaway greenhouse.

facts.claim: The planet has no moon; the only tide is a solar tide of order one metre.
facts.justification: At 0.52 AU the Hill sphere is small and any close moon would be tidally braked within a few hundred million years, so the equilibrium solar bulge is a rounding error and cannot explain flooding, migration timing or joint wear.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: No tidal mixing: coastal and pan flooding comes from seasonal evaporation and rare storms only.
Nights are moonless and starlit, so half of every 34-hour cycle belongs to hearing and smell.
Without a stabilising moon the axial tilt is free to wander (see F6).

facts.claim: The planet has a radius of 5,900 km, a mass of 0.67 Earth masses, a density of 4.65 g/cm³ and a surface gravity of 7.65 m/s² (0.78 g), with a 9.5 km/s escape velocity.
facts.justification: Radius, mass, density, gravity and escape velocity are one self-consistent set derived from a small iron core and a silicate mantle; low gravity is what makes a large rolling body cheap to build and cheap to keep moving.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Rolling and balling bodies can be large without crushing their own joints.
Dust settles slowly and hangs for days, so the air is usually dirty.
Lifting work per kilogram is 22% cheaper than on Earth, which favours gliding and burrowing too.

facts.claim: The day is 34 hours long, and the Coriolis force is about 0.7 times Earth's.
facts.justification: Slow rotation gives a weak Coriolis parameter, so weather organises into a few huge, sluggish systems instead of many small ones, and the dominant engine becomes the day-night heating pulse rather than planetary waves.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Long dawns and dusks with low, raking light and long shadows.
One enormous diurnal thermal wind combs the flats clean each rotation.
Storm systems are rare but continent-sized when they occur.

facts.claim: Axial tilt is currently about 21° but wanders chaotically between 8° and 38° on a cycle of order 0.4 million years.
facts.justification: Without a large moon to damp precession, spin-axis chaos is the default result of Mars/Laskar-class models, but the exact 8–38° amplitude and 0.4 Myr period are highly speculative here because they scale with an unknown precession constant; within a lifetime, a season or a game, tilt is effectively constant.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Seasonal structure is stable for lifetimes but not for evolution: the road network has a birth and a death date.
High-obliquity episodes push the subtropical dry belt over the shallow seas, exposing new Lanes.
Lineages specialised on the Lanes are living on borrowed time, and the fossil record says so.

facts.claim: A small iron dynamo gives a 0.4 gauss dipole, and cooled magnetite-rich basalt flows carry local remanent anomalies of 50–500 nT, rising to a few microtesla over the richest flows.
facts.justification: A small core supports a weak but real field well inside planetary norms, and flood basalt genuinely records that field, but bulk crustal remanence is nT to hundreds of nT — a uniform 0.15 gauss would be a magnetic ore body, not a rock — so the readable map is local and patchy.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Cosmic-ray dose is about 0.8 times Earth's, shielded mainly by the 1.5-bar air column.
Magnetotactic organs can navigate by rock remanence where landmarks fail.
A fresh flow erases the local map, so navigation knowledge decays.

facts.claim: Surface pressure is 1.5 bar: 77% N₂, 13% O₂ (0.195 bar), 1.1% CO₂, 5.2% Ar and 0.1-3% H₂O, giving a density of 1.86 kg/m³ and a scale height of 10.5 km.
facts.justification: Density follows from pM/RT at 286 K and scale height from RT/Mg at low gravity; O₂ at 0.195 bar is breathable but below Earth's, and argon is a passive tracer from potassium-rich basalt.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Fire is possible but sluggish, so combustion is not a dominant hazard.
Air drag at speed is 1.5 times Earth's, so fast rollers must be streamlined.
A 1.5-bar column is a decent cosmic-ray shield.

facts.claim: Sound travels at 339 m/s regardless of pressure, and in 1.5-bar air carries modestly farther than on Earth at the same pitch, of order 1.2-1.5× and strongly frequency-dependent.
facts.justification: Sound speed is √(γRT/M) and is pressure-independent; pressure only sets attenuation, and because molecular and turbulence losses vary with frequency the range gain is approximate rather than a clean 1.4×.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Low-frequency calls cross kilometres of flat ground.
Hearing becomes the primary long-range sense and stealth becomes almost impossible.
Anything that deafens, such as a sharp whistle above 6 kHz, is a weapon.

facts.claim: Rainfall averages 180 mm a year, and the main weather engine is a diurnal thermal wind of 9 m/s mean with 35 m/s spring gusts.
facts.justification: Deep day-night heating over dark rock drives a basin-scale circulation once per 34-hour rotation; with almost no mud and little rain, wind rather than water is the sculptor of the surface.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Scent posts persist for days, making smell a durable information layer.
Dust storms blind the flats in spring and erase tracks.
Surfaces are polished rather than eroded into soil, keeping the Lanes hard.

facts.claim: Topographically closed, wind-sheltered hollows can pool 5-12% CO₂ overnight, a hypoxic and lethal layer that persists only through the still hour or three around dawn.
facts.justification: CO₂ at 44 g/mol is heavier than 29 g/mol air and drains into closed basins, but 5-12% is far above the 1.1% bulk, so it needs local degassing vents or long prior pooling, and the daily thermal wind scours it out by mid-morning.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Some hollows are invisible dead zones at dawn and harmless by noon.
Concentrations above 5% cause headache, confusion and rapid unconsciousness in anything that breathes air.
Route timing matters as much as route choice.

facts.claim: Water covers 34% of the surface at a mean depth of 1.8 km, about 0.2 Earth oceans, in one polar sea and two rift seas.
facts.justification: The water budget is small enough that most of the planet is dry land with an endorheic interior, the precondition for enormous evaporite pans; a larger ocean would drown the Lanes.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Fresh water is a scarce resource held by legged species at oases.
The interior is a closed basin where salts and toxins accumulate.
Most of the world is desert pavement, not sea.

facts.claim: Relief is extremely low: 90% of land lies within 600 m of sea level and the highest point is 3.1 km, on a stagnant lid with no collisional mountains.
facts.justification: Without plate recycling or continental collision nothing builds ranges, so effusive flows and sediment fill dominate and horizons stay open for hundreds of kilometres.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Sight lines run to the horizon, so ambush depends on terrain texture and light, not hills.
Nothing forces water to run off, so basins become evaporite traps.
Weather systems cross the interior without orographic interruption.

facts.claim: Six flood-basalt provinces and about 20 million years of evaporite pans form the Lanes: flat, hard, wind-polished surfaces running for hundreds of kilometres with under a metre of relief.
facts.justification: Low-viscosity effusive basalt self-levels into sheet flows, endorheic evaporation indurates salt and gypsum crusts, and aeolian abrasion polishes both into pavement that resists burial.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Wheeled and balled locomotion is cheap on the Lanes and ruinous off them.
The Lanes form a connected graph, so geography becomes routing.
Pans are thin: a crust can hide brine or a void a few centimetres down.

facts.claim: Sea water sits at pH 7.9 while pan brines reach pH 9-10, concentrating selenate and arsenate to roughly 2 mg Se/kg along with fluoride from fresh ash.
facts.justification: Evaporative concentration raises ionic strength and pH and collects the soluble oxyanions of selenium and arsenic, as in Death Valley and Salton-type playas; the 2 mg/kg threshold is approximate and depends on the local mineral assemblage, but the direction is certain and makes off-Lane ground chemically hostile as well as rough.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Drinking from the wrong pan is lethal; halophiles must detoxify or volatilise.
Off-road travel is a chemical hazard, not just a traction penalty.
Salt itself is both resource and poison, depending on dose.

facts.claim: Energy enters the biosphere through far-red photosynthesis using pigments absorbing ~700-750 nm (the chlorophyll f class, near 720 nm) on wet salt and fresh basalt, plus Fe²⁺ and S⁰ chemolithotrophy, with wind and thermal gradients as physical subsidies.
facts.justification: An oxidising, iron- and sulphur-rich basaltic surface offers abundant redox couples, and a red star pushes photosynthesis to long wavelengths — the trick chlorophyll f already manages at the edge of the visible — so the food web does not depend on visible-light brightness and follows directly from F1's spectrum.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Primary production is patchy and tied to moisture, so grazers must migrate.
Chemolithotrophic films let life persist under crust and in lava channels.
Detritivores that eat shed keratin and salt crust close the loop.

facts.claim: Wheeled locomotion evolved in four usable steps: whole-body balling, a rolling dispersal cyst, a rotatable foot with a free-spinning dead cap, and finally a driven axle with a moulted tyre.
facts.justification: Each step pays for itself alone, which is what an evolutionary intermediate must do; a free axle cannot be fed, cooled or repaired, and the only rotary axle biology has built is the bacterial flagellar motor, which turns a filament inside a membrane and cannot scale into a load-bearing joint. Steps three and four are highly speculative (Gould essay 1981, collected 1983).

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Balling and cysts are common; true wheels are rare and recent.
Every wheeled lineage retains the ancestral balling escape.
Wheel anatomy is a stack of historical compromises, not an engineered design.

facts.claim: The karrow runs on a dead keratin-mineral tyre mounted on a vascularised collar and driven by friction pads on the tyre's inner rim, giving 3.2 times walking speed on a Lane.
facts.justification: If the rotating part is dead there is no vascular problem to solve: it is grown like a hoof or antler, fed through the collar while stationary and replaced by moult, and the living pads press on a dry rim so the motor never crosses the joint; the 'hundreds of kilometres' tyre life is speculative because it depends on an unmeasured abrasion rate.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Rolling resistance rises about tenfold in dust or brine, and a 12 cm step stops the animal dead.
Tyres wear out and must be regrown, so range is set by moult cycle, not fuel.
Discarded tyres litter the Lanes and attract scavengers and predators that read their residual heat.

facts.claim: The tucket escapes by curling its whole body into a wheel with no axle at all, reaching twice its running speed downhill but unable to see or steer while rolled.
facts.justification: Balling sidesteps the joint problem entirely and is attested on Earth in pangolins, armadillos and the wheel spider, and it pays off where a slope and a hard surface exist together, which is exactly a drying pan.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Balling is a defensive and dispersal reflex, not a way of life.
A rolled animal is committed: it cannot choose where it stops.
Predators learn to wait at the bottom of the slope.

facts.claim: A vascular sphincter clamps the axle as a brake and sweat glands dump the heat by evaporation, leaving a hot, scent-marked skid line about 40 m long after a 12 m/s stop.
facts.justification: Twelve metres per second of kinetic energy has to go somewhere, and in dry air evaporation is the only heat sink, so a wet, hot, smelly trace is the unavoidable physical residue of stopping at a few metres per second squared.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Stopping breaks a chase and simultaneously broadcasts where you stopped.
Still air causes heat exhaustion, so braking is weather-dependent.
Skid lines are readable history for anything that can smell.

facts.claim: Steering is passive: the axle trails the limb pivot by about 0.3 wheel radii, giving straight-line stability with a minimum turn radius near 4 m.
facts.justification: Caster geometry is a solved mechanical problem needing no neural loop, which matters because a 100 ms reflex at 12 m/s is already 1.2 m of travel; the price is a turning circle wider than a predator's.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Rollers run straight without attention and cannot corner tightly.
Switchbacks and broken ground belong to legged hunters.
Sharp course changes require shedding speed first.

facts.claim: Wheeled lineages keep two short walking legs and a lifting shoulder, and can stow the wheel and walk in about two seconds.
facts.justification: The Lanes are islands separated by dune seas and broken crust, and a wheel in loose sand is a trap rather than a vehicle; retaining legs is cheaper than evolving them twice, so the off-road answer is portage.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Crossing 200 m of dune costs roughly eight times the time it takes on a Lane.
The two-second transition is a real vulnerability window in combat.
Lane specialists and generalists diverge behaviourally, not just anatomically.

facts.claim: The tyre tread is farmed: a lichen-like symbiont grows the rolling surface and trades micronutrients and moisture with the host, producing a new tyre in about nine days.
facts.justification: Keratin wears out and the pans are nutrient-poor, so a tread that pays rent in micronutrients and water is worth feeding — the same loose bargain as algae in sloth fur; the arrangement is highly speculative, the exchange is documented as nutrient/moisture rather than verified nitrogen fixation, and the nine-day regrowth is an unconstrained ecological number.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Grooming and feeding the symbiont becomes daily husbandry.
The symbiont is the vector for a treadworm that lays eggs in dead tread.
A starved host loses its tyre before it loses its life.

facts.claim: Magnetite organs read the remanent anomalies of the basalt flows, giving position to about 0.5-2 km along a stripe and 100-500 m across it without landmarks.
facts.justification: A featureless white flat removes every visual cue but the rock underneath carries a weak magnetic map; magnetotaxis is real in bacteria and magnetite-based magnetoreception is documented in animals, so the sense is plausible while the precision follows from F7's nT-to-µT gradients rather than a strong field.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Navigation is a skill of reading geology, not scenery.
New flows and deep dust erase the map locally.
Two animals can disagree about where they are and both be honest.

facts.claim: Long-range communication uses 40-90 Hz hums that carry up to about 400 m in calm air, and the same ears are deaf above 6 kHz.
facts.justification: Low frequencies barely attenuate in 1.5-bar air and propagate well through hard ground, so the acoustic niche sits at the bottom of the spectrum; 400 m is optimistic and only holds in still air, and the cost is a hearing range that stops far below the whistles and clicks a rival can use.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Herds coordinate over hundreds of metres while staying silent to each other's rivals.
A sharp high whistle is a disabling weapon against anything with these ears.
Wind noise, not distance, sets the practical limit.

facts.claim: The glissen skates on the shallow ice of polar and high-latitude rift lakes on stiff legs and a single keratin blade, moving four times faster than a roller for the 20-50 days the ice lasts.
facts.justification: Ice has almost no rolling resistance and no traction either, so wheels cannot brake or steer on it while a blade can; only high-latitude, shallow, wind-sheltered lakes freeze long enough at 21° of tilt for a road to exist, which is why the winter road appears at the poles and never on the subtropical flats.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Territory changes hands seasonally without a fight.
Blades are useless in summer and shatter off ice.
Ice is a road that expires, so routes must be re-planned.

facts.claim: The Lanes support four exploiter guilds: sumpers tap hollow crust and dig 2 m sinkholes, skirls stoop at 30 m/s from height onto rollers, hub leeches attach to passing bodies, and hitchhiker spores ride the low-pressure boundary layer of anything fast.
facts.justification: A road concentrates traffic, and a thin salt crust plus a fast-moving cylinder is a predictable ambush geometry; the 30 m/s figure is a stoop from height, peregrine-class, not a level cruise, and the boundary layer of a rolling body genuinely draws in airborne propagules.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Infestation reduces rolling efficiency and attracts host-specific predators.
Sinkholes are cheap to make and expensive to find.
A grounded flyer is a meal, which is why skirls strike once.

facts.claim: The lye drinks brine of up to 350 g salt per kg of solution (about 26% w/w), volatilises selenium as dimethyl selenide, and must reach fresh water within about three days.
facts.justification: Brine is the only water for a hundred kilometres, and biomethylation of selenium to a volatile gas is a real microbial detoxification route; but above roughly 300 g NaCl per kg of solution a drinker cannot gain net water without excreting a fluid saltier than the pan, so saturated pans are for mining, not drinking, and the three-day limit is ecological, not physical.

provenance.council: planet drafts + peer reviews + astrobio referee, merged by the chair (deepseek skeptic)

consequences: Oases are held by legged species, so the fastest animals cannot drink.
Brine tolerance buys range and costs endurance.
Selenium breath makes the drinker smell like garlic and gives it away.
